parts.problem_md: Explain **one** reason why a business might change its organisational structure.
parts.solution_md:
One reason a business might change its structure is that it has grown **[1]**. A structure that worked when the owner supervised everyone directly becomes unworkable once there are too many employees for one person to manage **[1]**. Adding layers of management, or grouping staff into departments, shares supervision out, so decisions are made by people close enough to the work to understand it rather than being delayed while everyone waits for one overloaded manager **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Structures change in response to growth, changes in objectives, new technology, competitive pressure, cost-cutting, or a merger or takeover
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Growth eventually makes a single manager's span of control unworkable, so extra levels or departments are needed to share supervision
> - A business seeking faster decisions may remove management levels, shortening the chain of command so front-line staff can act without waiting for approval
> - New technology can make layers of middle management unnecessary, since information now passes directly between senior managers and front-line staff
> - A merger creates duplicate departments, so the combined business must reorganise to avoid paying twice for the same function
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The question asks why a structure changes, so name the trigger rather than describing the new structure. Growth, a merger, new technology and cost pressure are triggers; becoming flatter or adding departments is the response. Starting with the cause keeps your answer pointed at the question asked.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Greenway (GW)**
> 
> Greenway (GW) maintains parks and business grounds in country F. It employs 140 people working in 18 teams across the country.
> 
> GW's owner, Marcus, requires every team leader to send him photographs of completed work and to telephone him before buying materials costing more than \$50.
> 
> Team leaders say the calls waste time, particularly when a job needs a part urgently. Three team leaders have left in the past year, two of them saying they were not trusted to do their jobs.
> 
> Marcus says he has seen work done badly in the past and cannot risk GW's reputation.

Explain **one** conflict between control and trust in the way Marcus delegates.
parts.solution_md:
One conflict is that the checks Marcus uses to protect quality also signal that he does not trust his team leaders **[1]**. Requiring a telephone call before any purchase over \$50, and photographs of every completed job, means team leaders cannot act without approval even when a job needs a part urgently **[1]**. Two of the three team leaders who left last year said they were not trusted, so the controls Marcus uses to protect GW's reputation are costing him the experienced staff who protect that reputation day to day **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Delegation requires a manager to give subordinates authority while retaining accountability, which creates tension between controlling the work and trusting those who do it
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Requiring approval for purchases over \$50 keeps Marcus in control of spending but stops team leaders acting quickly when a job needs a part urgently
> - Photographing every completed job reassures Marcus about quality, yet signals to team leaders that their own judgement is not accepted
> - Two of the three team leaders who left cited a lack of trust, so the controls are driving out exactly the experienced staff Marcus depends on
> - Marcus's concern is not unreasonable, since poor work has damaged GW before, and with 18 teams spread across the country he cannot supervise directly
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A question about conflict needs both sides in your answer. Explaining only that the controls annoy staff, or only that Marcus has good reason for them, gives half the picture. Name what the control achieves and what it costs, then show why the two cannot both be fully satisfied.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** difference between a line function and a staff function.
parts.solution_md:
A line function is one that contributes directly to producing and selling the business's output, such as production or sales **[1]**. A staff function supports the line functions with specialist advice or services, such as human resources or legal **[1]**. The difference matters because line managers hold authority over the people below them in their own chain of command, whereas staff specialists usually advise rather than instruct, which can cause friction if their advice is ignored **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Line functions contribute directly to producing and selling the product; staff functions provide specialist support and advice to those line functions
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A production manager holds line authority over production employees, and can instruct them directly as part of the chain of command
> - A human resources specialist advises on recruitment or discipline but does not usually have authority to direct production staff
> - Staff functions let expertise be shared across the whole business rather than duplicated within every department
> - Tension can arise where line managers treat staff advice as interference, particularly when the specialist has no authority to insist
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A difference question needs a point of contrast, not two separate descriptions. Say what line functions do, say what staff functions do, then state what actually separates them, which here is authority. Answers describing each in turn without naming the difference tend to stop at two marks.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Fairstone (FS)**
> 
> Fairstone (FS) is an insurance company in country Y employing 2,400 people. It has nine levels of hierarchy between the chief executive and the staff who deal with customers.
> 
> A customer wanting to claim more than \$5,000 must have the claim approved at four separate levels.
> 
> FS's average time to settle a claim is 34 days. Two newer insurance companies in country Y settle claims in under a week, and have taken 6% of FS's market share in three years.

Explain **one** drawback to FS of its hierarchical structure.
parts.solution_md:
One drawback is that decisions take a long time to reach **[1]**. FS has nine levels between the chief executive and customer-facing staff, and a claim above \$5,000 must be approved at four separate levels **[1]**. Every approval adds waiting time, which is why FS takes 34 days to settle a claim while two newer insurers manage it in under a week; those competitors have already taken 6% of FS's market share, so the delay built into the structure is costing FS customers **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A tall hierarchical structure has many levels of management, long chains of command and narrow spans of control
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Four approval levels for claims above \$5,000 lengthen the time before a customer is paid, producing an average of 34 days against under a week at newer rivals
> - Nine levels between chief executive and front-line staff mean information travels slowly in both directions, so senior managers may learn of problems only after customers have left
> - Employees dealing with customers have little authority, which may reduce their motivation and their willingness to resolve problems themselves
> - Many management levels are expensive, as each carries salaries and overheads the flatter newer competitors do not have to cover
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A drawback question needs you to say who or what suffers as a result. Here it is not simply that decisions are slow; it is that customers wait 34 days, rivals settle in under a week, and FS has lost 6% of the market. Following the drawback through to its victim is what earns the third mark.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Rosemont (RM)**
> 
> Rosemont (RM) manufactures skincare products in country H. It employs 260 people and sells to pharmacies and department stores.
> 
> RM is organised into four departments: production, marketing, finance, and human resources. Each is led by a director who reports to the managing director.
> 
> Staff in each department work only within their own specialism. RM's chemists all sit within production, and its designers all sit within marketing.
> 
> RM's managing director says the arrangement means she always knows who is responsible for what.

Explain **one** benefit to RM of a functional structure.
parts.solution_md:
One benefit is that RM's specialists work alongside others doing the same kind of work **[1]**. All of RM's chemists sit within production and all of its designers within marketing, so each group can share knowledge and solve problems together **[1]**. In a business making skincare products, where formulation expertise takes years to build, keeping chemists together means less experienced staff learn from more experienced colleagues, which raises the standard of RM's products over time **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A functional structure groups employees by the type of work they do, such as production, marketing, finance and human resources, each headed by a specialist director
> 
> AO2
> 
> - All RM's chemists sit within production, so expertise is concentrated and less experienced staff learn from colleagues doing the same work
> - Each of the four departments has a director accountable for it, which is why RM's managing director always knows who is responsible for what
> - Grouping by function avoids duplicating roles, since RM needs only one finance team rather than a separate one for each product line
> - Clear departmental boundaries give employees an obvious career path within their specialism, helping RM retain skilled chemists and designers
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A benefit of a structure is really a statement about how work gets done. Rather than calling a functional structure "organised" or "efficient", say what it lets people actually do: share expertise, avoid duplication, know who decides. Naming the mechanism is where the development marks are.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'decentralisation'.
parts.solution_md:
Decentralisation is when decision-making authority is passed from senior managers at the centre of a business **[1]** to managers in its divisions, branches or regions **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The transfer of decision-making authority away from head office to lower levels or local units
> - An arrangement where branches, divisions or regions decide matters themselves rather than referring them upwards
> - Spreading authority through the organisation so decisions are taken closer to where their effects are felt

> **[exam-tip]**
> A term beginning with "de-" tempts students to answer "the opposite of centralisation", which earns nothing. Define it in its own right: authority for decisions moves from the centre out to divisions or branches. Examiners want the idea itself, not a cross-reference to another term.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'matrix structure'.
parts.solution_md:
A matrix structure is an organisational structure in which employees are grouped into project teams **[1]** while also belonging to their usual department, so they report to two managers **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A structure in which staff work in cross-functional project teams while retaining a place in their own department
> - An arrangement where an employee answers both to a departmental head and to a project leader
> - A structure combining functional and project reporting lines, so authority runs in two directions at once

> **[exam-tip]**
> Structure questions reward a description of the shape. For a matrix, the defining feature is two reporting lines: a department and a project. Saying employees "work together in teams" describes almost any structure, so name the dual reporting to make clear which one you mean.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'authority'.
parts.solution_md:
Authority is the power a person holds within a business to make decisions and instruct others **[1]**, given to them by the position they occupy in the organisational structure **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The right to make decisions, allocate resources and give instructions, arising from a person's position in the hierarchy
> - Legitimate power held by a post holder to direct the work of others and to commit the business's resources
> - The formal ability to require action from subordinates, granted by the organisation rather than earned personally

> **[exam-tip]**
> Authority and responsibility are usually taught together, so it is tempting to define both. This question asks for one. Define authority, the right to decide and instruct, and leave responsibility alone. Answering more than was asked costs time without adding marks.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'delegation'.
parts.solution_md:
Delegation is when a manager passes authority to carry out a task to a subordinate **[1]**, while remaining accountable for whether the task is completed properly **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Passing authority for a task down to a more junior employee, with the manager still answerable for the outcome
> - Giving a subordinate the power to make decisions about a piece of work, without transferring ultimate responsibility for it
> - Entrusting work to someone lower in the hierarchy, together with the authority needed to complete it

> **[exam-tip]**
> The examiner is looking for what does and does not transfer. Authority passes to the subordinate; accountability stays with the manager. Getting that asymmetry into your definition secures the second mark, and it is the point students most often get wrong on this topic.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'span of control'.
parts.solution_md:
Span of control is the number of employees who report directly to one manager **[1]**, and it determines how many people that manager is responsible for supervising **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The number of subordinates directly answerable to a single manager
> - A measure of how many employees one manager supervises directly, which affects how closely each can be monitored
> - The count of people immediately below a manager in the chain of command, described as wide when large and narrow when small

> **[exam-tip]**
> Span of control is a number, so your definition should make clear what is being counted: the employees reporting directly to one manager. The word "directly" matters, because people further down the chain are not part of that manager's span even though they sit below them.

> - Decentralisation means passing decision-making authority down the organisation to empower managers in functional areas or regional divisions to take decisions that would otherwise be made at head office.
> - Decentralising decision-making gives managers closer to the market the authority to respond quickly to competitive threats and local opportunities; KB is expanding into country Q, where demand for healthy drinks is growing rapidly, and also faces growing pressure from MNCs in the domestic market
> - Managers with authority to act immediately - for example, adjusting promotional strategies or responding to competitor pricing - can help KB capitalise on opportunities and defend market share more effectively than a centralised structure would permit
> - However, fast local decisions are only beneficial if managers have sufficient strategic understanding to make good choices, and without the full picture that Lily holds, some decisions may be suboptimal and waste KB's limited resources

parts.solution_md:
A decentralised structure passes decision-making authority from senior managers to lower levels of the hierarchy **[K]**. For HBG, this means removing three layers of middle management and giving local property managers more authority over marketing and operations **[Ap]**

The main benefit is that HBG will be able to respond more quickly to new ideas and opportunities **[K]**. Under the current structure, local managers reported frustration at how long it took to get decisions approved by HQ **[Ap]**. Giving property managers the authority to act locally - for example, creating events to attract international tourists, identified as a key opportunity in the SWOT analysis - means HBG can respond to market changes without waiting for head office approval **[An]**

Decentralisation is also likely to reduce HBG's labour turnover **[K]**, which has averaged 11% per year **[Ap]**. Employees currently feel they are given orders without explanation and have little real responsibility. Giving staff more authority should make them feel more trusted and valued, improving motivation and reducing the number who leave **[An]**

However, removing three layers of management will result in redundancies **[K]**, which conflicts directly with HBG's new commitment to improving its corporate social responsibility **[Ap]**. Simultaneously making employees redundant and emphasising CSR could damage HBG's reputation and reduce trust among remaining staff **[An]**

There is also a risk that local managers make decisions that harm HBG's brand **[K]** - with over 200 properties **[Ap]**, inconsistent standards could confuse customers and undermine the high brand awareness that is one of HBG's key strengths **[An]**

On balance, decentralisation is likely to benefit HBG, since the current centralised structure is clearly not working **[E]** - membership is falling and both employees and customers are dissatisfied **[Ap]**. However, the HR Director's concerns about training are valid **[E]**. An organisational structure shows how a business is organised and who makes decisions **[K]**. I recommend that JGS uses a hierarchical functional structure, where Jan and Gorl remain in overall control but delegate some operational authority to the three new regional managers **[E]**

In this structure, JGS employees would be grouped into clear functions - such as administration, marketing, guiding, and accommodation - with Jan and Gorl at the top of the hierarchy, regional managers in the middle, and operational staff below **[Ap]**. Having a clear structure means every employee knows exactly who they report to and what they are responsible for **[An]**. This also makes it easier for JGS to show that it is meeting the new country P employment regulations, since Jan and Gorl can see clearly which regional manager is responsible for which employees and whether legal standards are being followed **[An]**

Jan and Gorl should keep control of the most important strategic decisions, such as pricing, CSR standards, and marketing **[Ap] [E]**. This is important because JGS has built a reputation for responsible and high-quality tours, which is a key reason customers choose JGS over other businesses **[Ap]**. As more competitors enter the market, maintaining consistent standards is essential. A centralised approach to strategy means Jan and Gorl can ensure that JGS's values and policies are applied in the same way across all tours **[An]**

However, regional managers must be given some delegated authority **[K] **to make operational decisions on the ground. Guides and host families work in mountain villages that are not accessible by road **[Ap]**, so Jan and Gorl cannot always be reached quickly when problems arise. Giving regional managers the authority to respond to situations - for example, replacing a guide who is unable to lead a walk - means customers are not affected by delays **[An]**

It allows Jan to maintain the strategic control he wants, while ensuring that operational problems in remote locations can be resolved quickly **[Ap]**. >

This would be beneficial for WTZ because the business has grown through diversification - each product serves a different market with different customers and competitors. It would also reduce the pressure on Amandi, who currently struggles to maintain effective control as the business grows into new areas. Divisional managers would be empowered to lead their own teams, which could increase motivation and improve performance **[An]**

This brings together employees from different departments, such as operations and marketing, to work together on new products **[K]**. WTZ's two most successful innovations, the Hydrocamel and the recycled plastic bricks **[Ap]**, required expertise from across the business. A matrix structure would make this kind of cross-functional teamwork easier and more regular, helping WTZ to continue innovating **[An]**

However, there is a risk that Amandi may be reluctant to give up control to divisional managers, which could limit the effectiveness of the change **[E]**.
